title: *you can do this*
hook: a calendar with five limbs, a moon that sets the dates, and nobody who keeps every festival

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second half of Pongal Onam: a flower carpet growing at the door for a king who comes home once a year. What did you get ready? Today, the whole year, and how to hold it. Day one hundred fifty-five.

In the last two and a half weeks you've been through a lot of festivals. Five days of Diwali. Holi's fire and colors. Nine nights of Navaratri. A midnight cradle. A clay Ganesha, welcomed and let go. A night awake for Shiva. A thread. Kites. A pot boiling over. A king coming home. If you're feeling a small wave of panic, that's fair. How is anyone supposed to keep all of that? Here's the honest answer, and it's a relief. Almost nobody does.
screen: `TEN FESTIVALS IN THREE WEEKS.` → `HOW DOES ANYONE KEEP ALL THAT?` → `ALMOST NOBODY DOES.`

segments.voice: Start with how the year is counted. Most of these festivals are set by the moon. A Hindu month has a bright half, as the moon grows, and a dark half, as it shrinks, and each lunar day is called a tithi. Janmashtami is the eighth of the dark half. Ganesh Chaturthi is the fourth of the bright half. That's why the dates move around your wall calendar every year. Every so often an extra month is added, so the moon's year doesn't drift too far from the seasons. And there are a few solar days, like Makar Sankranti, that stay put. To find the dates, families use a panchang, an almanac. The word means five limbs: the lunar day, the weekday, the star the moon is passing, and two more ways of dividing time. Many families have a printed one on the kitchen wall; now there are apps. Second thing: nobody keeps them all. A family in Kolkata lives for Durga Puja. A family in Pune lives for Ganesha. In Kerala it's Onam; in Tamil Nadu, Pongal. Families keep what their region, their parents and their temple keep, and add what they love. That isn't doing it wrong. That's how it has always been done. Third: a festival doesn't need to be big to count. A lamp on Diwali. A pinch of color on Holi. Staying up one watch on Shivaratri. One thread. The tradition itself is full of small, real ways in. So here's what this whole camp has been saying, in one line. You don't have to do everything. You have to do something, on purpose, and do it again next year.
screen: `THE MOON SETS THE DATES.` · `A PANCHANG: THE FIVE LIMBS.` · `NOBODY KEEPS THEM ALL.` · `SMALL COUNTS.` · then, large: `SOMETHING, ON PURPOSE, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your three. Settle, and breathe. Let the festivals pass through your mind like floats in a parade. Diwali's lamps. Holi's colors. Navaratri's nine nights. The midnight cradle. Ganesha in clay. The Shivaratri vigil. The rakhi. Kites. The pot. The flower carpet. Don't decide yet. Just notice which ones made something in you lean forward. Now pick three. Only three. For each, picture the smallest real way you could keep it this year. One lamp. One watch. One thread. Hold your three. The bell holds the time.
You can do this. Not all of it. Something, on purpose, the next time the moon comes round.
Your line: you can do this. Today, look up when your first of the three falls this year, and put it in your calendar. Day one hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Most Hindu families keep the festivals their region, family and temple keep, finding the lunar dates each year in a panchang, a printed almanac or app, and marking them at home in small ways as well as large.

what it means: nobody keeps them all. families keep what's theirs, small or large, and do it again next year.
what a scholar hears: tithi, vara, nakshatra, yoga, karana: the panchang's five limbs, with an extra month added now and then to stay with the seasons.

sources.ref: The Hindu lunisolar calendar: tithi, paksha, adhika masa; the panchanga's five limbs

notes: Panchanga's five limbs: tithi, vara, nakshatra, yoga, karana. Voiced as 'the lunar day, the weekday, the star the moon is passing, and two more ways of dividing time'. Confirm.
Adhika masa (intercalary month) roughly every 32–33 months; written as 'every so often'. Confirm.
The hook lists Diwali as five days (days 139–140, written by another writer); confirm consistency with those scripts.
